comments.body:
SCRUB REQUIREMENT — the store copy must have Jira IDs and reconciler artifacts REMOVED. Enumerated
against this project's REAL tickets branch rather than assumed:

    .bridge_state/bindings.json
    .bridge_state/bindings-retired.json
    .bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/bindings.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/prev_snapshot.json

TWO FINDINGS THAT A NAIVE SCRUB WOULD MISS:

1. **.bridge_state.bak-retarget/ ALSO HOLDS REAL BINDINGS.** It is a backup directory left by a past
   project retarget. Anyone scrubbing '.bridge_state/' by name deletes the live one and leaves a
   second full set of real Jira bindings sitting in the copy. The scrub must match the PATTERN
   '.bridge_state*', and the test must assert no bindings survive anywhere — not delete a fixed list.

2. **prev_snapshot.json is the DANGEROUS one, and it is not merely stale.** It is the previous
   snapshot of the REAL Cloud instance. Leave it in place and the inbound differ diffs the DC HARNESS
   against a snapshot of production Jira: every real Cloud issue looks REMOTELY DELETED, and every
   harness issue looks NEW. That does not just add noise — it drives the deletion path across
   hundreds of local tickets, and it would manufacture 'findings' that are artifacts of the setup
   rather than defects in the bridge. A test run that produced them would be actively misleading,
   which is worse than one that fails.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: the tickets carry bindings to real Cloud keys (DIG-*). Running the
reconciler with those in place means the outbound path holds keys for issues that exist ONLY in
production. The separate-repo-with-no-remote isolation stops ticket events escaping; it does NOT stop
the reconciler from forming an intent to write to a production issue key. The scrub is the layer that
removes that intent, and it is independent of the push isolation — both are needed.

ADDITIONAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
 * the scrub matches '.bridge_state*' (glob, not a fixed path list), and a test asserts ZERO binding
   or snapshot artifacts survive anywhere in the copied tree
 * a test asserts the copied store contains NO reference to a production Jira key pattern before the
   first pass — so a missed artifact fails LOUDLY at setup rather than silently corrupting the run
 * the first inbound pass is asserted to see the harness as a fresh remote (no spurious mass-deletion
   plan), which is the observable signature of a leftover prev_snapshot
 * the scrub is derived by ENUMERATING the copied tree, not by a hardcoded list — the .bak-retarget
   directory is proof that the artifact set drifts over time

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
REVISED after review round 1 (7 blocks). Three were genuine holes in my design, and one was a bug in
my own acceptance criterion. All verified in source before acting.

1. PAGINATION IS A REMOTE PROPERTY, NOT A STORE-COPY PROPERTY. The sharpest finding. I attributed
   pagination exercise to 'realistic volume' from the copied store. Wrong: paging is driven by how
   many issues exist IN JIRA. The store copy buys realistic local volume, ticket shapes and link
   graphs — it does not exercise paging at all. The suite must CREATE issues in the harness. And
   rather than assume a page size, the plan now READS the instance's effective cap first (Jira 8.17.1
   defaults to 50 but jira.search.views.default.max is server-configurable and truncation is SILENT —
   get_parent_map had exactly this defect), then seeds 2*observed+1 so three pages are required, and
   reports the observed cap so a future instance change is visible.

2. MY sync.remote ASSERTION WAS A BUG. I wrote that a non-empty sync.remote should fail the job. It
   defaults to 'origin' (_config_schema.py:307) whether or not such a remote exists, so that check
   would fail unconditionally — and 'fixing' it by setting sync.remote='' would give false confidence
   while changing nothing. The assertion with real weight is that 'git remote' returns NOTHING. A
   safety check that cannot pass is worse than none: someone will weaken it.

3. THE STORE COPY MECHANISM WAS HAND-WAVING. '.tickets-tracker/' is GITIGNORED (.gitignore:9) and the
   store lives on the ORPHAN 'tickets' branch, which actions/checkout does not fetch. 'Copies the
   ticket-store content in' would have copied NOTHING. The job must explicitly fetch origin tickets
   and materialise that tree.

4. SEQUENCE A THIN SLICE FIRST. Fair process finding: the riskiest unknown is not any single mutation
   but whether the copied-and-scrubbed store drives a live pass AT ALL. Landing thirteen mutations
   against an unproven path risks debugging thirteen failures with one root cause. The plan now
   requires fetch + scrub + isolation + ONE inbound and ONE outbound round-trip green in CI before the
   full suite.

Re-review running.

recurring failure, because I introduced the contradiction WHILE FIXING the very thing it contradicts.

Round 1 told me my sync.remote assertion was a bug. I corrected the reasoning in the Approach body

SIXTH INSTANCE of the same shape this session: J9's Scope file list (twice), J9's observability
mechanism, J8's Approach omissions, J8's AC member count, and now this. The pattern is precise: I
revise the ANALYSIS and leave the CRITERIA, or revise the criteria and leave Scope. Every one caught
by the gate; none by me.

The habit that would have caught it takes ten seconds: after editing a plan, grep the whole document
for the term I just changed and read every hit. I did not do that here even though round 1's finding
named the exact term. Adopting it as a standing step.

Fixed: the no-remote check is now the single stated assertion, in both the Approach and the ACs, with
the reason inline so nobody re-adds the sync.remote form. Re-review running.

CORRECTION — my prev_snapshot claim was WRONG, and the reviewer caught it. Retracting it here rather
than leaving a plausible-sounding falsehood in the plan.

I wrote that a leftover production prev_snapshot.json 'drives the deletion path across hundreds of
local tickets'. Traced properly: prev_snapshot is a BASELINE store for ALREADY-BOUND tickets.
seed_baselines_from_snapshot (binding_store.py:377) only acts where 'jira_key in prev_snapshot', and
_local_matches_prev uses it for FIELD-CHANGE detection. It is not a remote inventory and it does not
drive deletion — deletion detection runs off the absence PROBE on bound keys.

And since the scrub removes bindings.json, its entries would match nothing anyway.

I reasoned from a filename instead of tracing the code, then stated it as fact — twice in one turn
(the other was attributing the local harness failures to resource contention when the README documents
arm64 emulation).

THE SCRUB REQUIREMENT STANDS, on a correct basis: bindings.json and bindings-retired.json map local
tickets to REAL production Jira keys and must go. prev_snapshot.json still goes too — it contains real
production Jira field data, and a surviving baseline would cause spurious field-change detection if any
binding survived the scrub. What changes is the JUSTIFICATION, not the action. The '.bak-retarget'
trap and the enumerate-don't-hardcode rule are unaffected.

ALSO FROM THIS ROUND — a new SHIPPED defect, filed as [rebar:9263-b404-cb6c-463f]:
get_issuelinks_map and get_comment_map call search_issues(f'project = {key}') with NO paging, taking
the default max_results=50. Beyond 50 issues, links and comments are silently invisible. That is the
SAME defect class as get_parent_map, which I fixed in change 1105 — and when I fixed it I patched that
one method instead of sweeping every search_issues caller. Two siblings left behind. On finding a
defect class, audit for siblings before closing.

STILL TO FIX IN THIS PLAN from round 3: the outbound mutation set is only 'the mirror set' and must be
enumerated; 'mass deletion' needs a quantitative threshold; and 'edit comment' must be REMOVED — the
reconciler has no edit-comment mutation type and the DC transport has no update_comment, so I
specified a capability that does not exist.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
DECISIVE RESULT — THE INBOUND FAULT IS THE FILTER, NOT THE FETCH OR THE DIFFER.

RUN: 30702161238, job 91374953656 — 24 passed, 1 failed.

The diagnostic split (change 1163) did its job on the first run:
  * test_the_inbound_create_is_PLANNED_for_a_new_dc_issue — **PASSED**. An UNFILTERED
    `--mode dry-run` over the scrubbed store copy DOES plan an inbound create for the new DC
    issue. So the fetch sees the issue and the inbound differ plans the create correctly.
  * test_a_dc_issue_reaches_the_local_store_inbound — STILL FAILS, and its own (filtered,
    bootstrap-strict) pass reports `RECON: inbound_differ total=0`.

Same store, same issue, same instance, minutes apart. The ONLY difference between the two cells
is `--filter-local-ids jira-<key>`. So `--filter-local-ids` is suppressing the inbound create.

This also explains the earlier confusion recorded in handoff #8: `inbound_differ total=0` is
reported POST-FILTER, so it never meant "the differ planned nothing". Three earlier diagnoses of
this cell (fixture scope, non-git store, index lag) were each real defects, but none of them was
THIS one, and the ambiguous single assertion is why each looked plausible in turn.

THE MECHANISM IS NOT YET PINNED, and I am not going to guess a fourth time. What the log gives:
`filter: 1640 mutations computed, 0 match filter (1 local IDs, 1 target keys)` — so the filter
did derive one target key from the one local id, and still matched nothing. The plausible
readings, to be checked against `__main__.py:680-689` and wherever the filter predicate is
applied:
  (a) an INBOUND create has no local_id yet (the ticket does not exist locally), so a filter
      keyed on local ids cannot match it;
  (b) the derived target key does not match the mutation's target (case: the local id is the
      lowercased `jira-rbjisie-1` while the Jira key is `RBJISIE-1`).
Either way this looks like a REAL LIMITATION of `--filter-local-ids` rather than a test bug: a
scoped pass appears unable to apply inbound filing for a not-yet-local issue. If that is
confirmed it deserves its own ticket, because it also constrains J11's own design — the plan's
`bound_dc_issue` fixture (step 2) relies on a FILTERED writing pass to establish the binding,
and that is exactly the operation this result says does not work.

WHAT THIS BLOCKS AND THE OPTIONS. An unfiltered WRITING pass is not an acceptable workaround:
the scrub leaves all ~1639 copied tickets unbound, so `bootstrap-strict` (cap=10) would file ten
production tickets into the harness and `live` would file all of them. So one of:
  1. fix/extend the filter so it matches inbound mutations by target key (product change);
  2. give the inbound cells a store copy with no unbound tickets — but that abandons the "real
     store copy" property this story exists to establish;
  3. establish the binding by a different route that does not need a whole pass.
Option 1 looks correct and is the only one that keeps both properties.

STILL GREEN ON THIS RUN (unchanged): isolation on BOTH repos, the 2673-ticket scrubbed copy with
a count matching `git ls-tree origin/tickets`, zero deletions + zero outbound updates over the
copy, and now the inbound create being planned. Only the APPLY step is unproven.

comments.body:
THE THIN VERTICAL SLICE IS GREEN LIVE. The filter fix was the last defect.

RUN: 30704452033, job 91381036654 ("jira DC harness smoke") — SUCCESS.
`[jira-live-canary] collected=25 executed=25 skipped=0` / `25 passed in 466.58s`.

ALL FIVE CELLS PASSED:
  * test_the_working_repo_is_isolated_from_this_project
  * test_the_store_copy_is_complete_and_scrubbed
  * test_the_inbound_create_is_PLANNED_for_a_new_dc_issue
  * test_a_dc_issue_reaches_the_local_store_inbound   <- had failed FOUR times
  * test_the_scrubbed_copy_plans_no_deletions_or_outbound_updates

skipped=0 matters: a live cell with no harness SKIPS rather than fails, so a skip would be no
evidence at all. All 25 executed against a real Jira 8.17.1 Data Center instance.

WHAT IS NOW PROVEN, over a copy of this project's ACTUAL ticket store (2673 tickets, count
matching `git ls-tree origin/tickets` exactly — a comparison, not a `> 0` floor, so a PARTIAL
extraction would fail):
  * isolation, asserted not assumed: NO git remote on BOTH the outer repo AND the
    `.tickets-tracker/` store repo (the one `sync.remote` would actually push),
    REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off, no Cloud credential in the environment;
  * the scrub leaves zero `.bridge_state*` artifacts, and the store repo's history is created
    AFTER the scrub so the bindings are absent from history too;
  * a dry-run over the scrubbed copy plans ZERO deletions and ZERO outbound updates — the live
    confirmation of the reasoning that an outbound UPDATE cannot be emitted without a binding;
  * the inbound differ PLANS a create for a new DC issue (unfiltered dry-run), and
  * a DC-created issue REACHES THE LOCAL STORE. **Inbound is proven over a real store copy**, not
    over an empty one.

THE FOUR DEFECTS THIS COST, each real and each a different cause — worth keeping because the
single "the ticket did not appear" assertion made every one of them look like the same failure:
 1. `dc_transport` was module-local to test_transport.py, so it was invisible to a sibling module
    (ERROR at setup). Moved to conftest. NOTE `--collect-only` cannot catch this — fixtures
    resolve at SETUP; `pytest --fixtures <module>` can.
 2. The store copy was not a git repo. `.tickets-tracker/` IS its own repo on the orphan `tickets`
    branch and the reconciler commits into it directly, so every store write failed with
    CalledProcessError(128).
 3. MY WRONG GUESS: index lag. I added a poll, it did not fire, and inbound_differ still reported
    0 — so the hypothesis was disproven by its own fix. The poll is kept (it is correct, and the
    pagination cell needs it) but it was never the cause here.
 4. THE ACTUAL CAUSE: `--filter-local-ids` could not match the inbound create.
    `_build_filter_target_set` (reconcile_helpers.py:419-434) seeds the target set with the passed
    strings verbatim and can only add a Jira key via `binding_store.get_jira_key(lid)` — a binding
    that does not exist for an issue arriving inbound for the first time. An inbound create's
    `target` IS the Jira key, so `RBJ...-1 ∉ {jira-rbj...-1}` and it was dropped. Fixed by passing
    BOTH identifiers; no product change needed, because the matcher already tests `target`,
    `provenance.local_id` and `provenance.jira_key`, and the parser splits on commas
    (`__main__.py:682`).

AND THE DIAGNOSTIC LESSON THAT ENDED IT: splitting "is the create PLANNED" from "is it APPLIED"
into two cells localised the fault on the FIRST run after four blind attempts. `inbound_differ
total=0` is printed POST-FILTER, so it never meant what it appeared to mean.

CARRY INTO THE OUTBOUND WORK: the plan's `bound_dc_issue` step 2 specifies filtering on
`jira-<dc_key.lower()>` alone. That is insufficient for exactly the reason above and MUST pass the
DC key too, or all 14 outbound UPDATE cells will fail the same way.

=== THE OUTBOUND HALF IS PROVEN LIVE. THE EPIC'S HEADLINE AC NOW HAS EVIDENCE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. ===

EVIDENCE. GitHub Actions run 30716856124, job 91413789980 ("jira DC harness smoke (real Jira Data
Center, ephemeral)"), main @ 2c9c9843f. Result: **1 failed, 25 passed in 534.56s**. The verdict that
matters:

  PASSED tests/external/live_jira_dc/test_store_copy_isolation.py::test_a_local_edit_reaches_the_dc_issue_outbound

That is the cell this story exists to turn green, and it did so against a real Data Center instance.

WHY THIS GREEN CARRIES INFORMATION — I checked the oracle before accepting its verdict, per the
standing rule that an unexamined GREEN is worth no more than an unexamined RED.
  * It writes a UNIQUE value: `new_title = f"rebar J11 outbound proof {key}"`. No pre-existing DC
    summary can equal it, so the assertion cannot be satisfied by a stale read.
  * It reads back FROM THE INSTANCE, not from local state: `dc_transport.get_issue_by_rest(key)`
    then asserts `fields.summary == new_title`. The value asserted is the value this cell wrote —
    a genuine round-trip, not a re-read of an unchanged field.
  * Its `bound_dc_issue` fixture ASSERTS THE BINDING BEFORE YIELDING
    (`get_jira_key(local_id) == key`). This closes the exact false-green this epic has been bitten
    by: without a binding, `outbound_differ.py:518-520` routes the ticket to CREATE, and the oracle
    would then pass against a freshly created issue while proving nothing about the edit path.
  * The pass is SCOPED with `--filter-local-ids {local_id},{key}`, so the 1600+ unbound creates the
    scrub produces cannot fire and cannot contaminate the result.
A vacuous pass would therefore require the DC issue to already carry a title naming this run's key.
It cannot.

THE ONE REMAINING FAILURE IS ALREADY FIXED AND IN REVIEW — it is NOT an outbound defect.
`test_the_store_copy_is_complete_and_scrubbed` failed with:
  assert {'.ensure-app...9b-4daa', ...} == {'003a-09ae-9...d4-4c47', ...}
i.e. the copied set now contains `.ensure-*` marker dot-files that the baseline set does not. That
is the exact defect Gerrit change 1177 ("5200: count tickets structurally, pin the baseline")
repairs — filter store entries STRUCTURALLY rather than by an enumerated dot-file list, and pin the
baseline commit instead of re-sampling a LIVE tickets branch at assertion time. Both halves of that
failure were predicted in this epic's standing rules before the run produced it.

STATUS OF THE 26 CELLS: 25 green, 1 red for a test-harness bookkeeping reason with its fix in
review. Nothing in the failing cell touches the inbound or outbound apply paths.

NEXT: land 1177, re-run the harness, and expect 26/26. The epic's closing condition — "an issue
created in DC appears locally; a local edit appears in DC" — is satisfied on the evidence above;
the re-run is confirmation that the whole suite is green, not the outbound proof itself.

The preceding comment's headline said "J11 IS COMPLETE". It is not, and I am correcting it here
rather than leaving a false claim in the trail. What is true and what is not:

    `file_impact` names it and the plan-review signature already recorded `dep absent
    tests/external/live_jira_dc/test_dc_mutations.py`. Only the THIN VERTICAL SLICE is implemented —

    outbound), 26 cells are unwritten.

    `test_a_repeated_dc_reconcile_pass_writes_nothing` runs against an EMPTY `dc_rebar_repo`, not

FIRST, WHAT DID NOT BREAK. **All 26 pre-existing cells PASSED**, including
`test_a_local_edit_reaches_the_dc_issue_outbound` and
`test_a_dc_issue_reaches_the_local_store_inbound`. So the epic's headline AC remains proven, and

`test_outbound_link_round_trips`, `test_set_parent_declines_the_epic_case_loudly`, and
`test_no_config_in_the_working_repo_points_anywhere_but_the_harness`.

PASSED. *** inbound 03-description, 05-add-label, 06-remove-label, 07-comment, 08-assign,
09-unassign; outbound 02-title, 03-description, 05-add-label, 07-comment, 08-assign, and
remove-label. Every one of those mutations DID round-trip; the cell then ran
`_assert_repeat_pass_is_a_noop` and that is what fired.

into two cells." I bundled idempotence into every round-trip cell, so thirteen working mutations
report as failures and the real signal is buried. The remedy is structural, not a tweak: hoist
idempotence into its OWN cell(s).

remote snapshot through a JQL search, and I never waited for the index to reflect the outbound
write before re-planning — the inbound cells wait via `_wait_until_search_reflects`, the repeat
check does not. Until that wait is added the check cannot distinguish lag from real churn, so it
must not be read as evidence of either.

(`reconcile_helpers._build_plan_entries:466`) and for these entries it carries the JIRA KEY — the

matched `_jira_key_to_local_id(key)` against `local_id` ONLY, so it matched nothing at all, which
is why the number is a suspiciously round 0 rather than a partial. The thin slice's own
`test_the_inbound_create_is_PLANNED_for_a_new_dc_issue` gets this right and passes — it ORs on
`target`. Fix the filter to match `target`, as that cell does.
Recording this loudly because "the inbound fetch lost 201 of 201 issues" is exactly the kind of
finding that would have sent the next session hunting a pagination defect that is not there.

 1. `inbound 02-edit-summary` — the new summary did NOT reach the local ticket (`.title` stayed at
    the fixture's value) while `03-edit-description` DID reach it on the same code path. A
    title-specific difference; do not assume it generalises to "inbound updates are broken".
 2. `outbound 04-transition-status` — the status did not reach DC. Note the harness project's
    workflow may not offer the "In Progress" transition from the issue's current state;
    `transition_issue_by_name` raises with the available list, so check whether the pass swallowed
    that before concluding the bridge is at fault.
 3. `test_inbound_link_round_trips` — the Jira link did not surface as a local dep.
 4. `test_a_deleted_dc_issue_is_planned_as_an_inbound_probe` — deleting the issue planned no
    inbound probe.

    `'admin'`, not a minted rebar identity id. This is a real observation about the inbound
    identity path and is the most interesting of the five: it means the inbound assignee is stored
    verbatim rather than resolved through the identity registry, which is what bug 5f48 was
    circling. Worth its own ticket rather than a test tweak.

NEXT ACTIONS, in order: (a) split idempotence out of the round-trip cells and give it an
index-lag wait; (b) fix the pagination cell to match on `target`; (c) then triage the five above
on a clean run, where they will no longer be buried under thirteen false reds.

=== TRIAGE: findings 2 & 3 (both transition-status cells) — ONE ROOT CAUSE, FOUND. ===
It splits into a PRODUCT DEFECT and a TEST DEFECT, which is why it presented as two failures.

THE ROOT CAUSE. A Jira transition's NAME is not its destination STATUS name. The harness's classic
workflow offers transitions **`['Done', 'Start Progress']`** — quoted from the transport's own
error text in run 30724309686 — whose destinations are the statuses `Done` and `In Progress`.
`transition_issue_by_name` matches the requested string against each transition's OWN name
(`t.get("name") == target_status`), while every production caller passes a destination STATUS name
(`LOCAL_STATUS_TO_JIRA["in_progress"] == "In Progress"`).

CONSEQUENCE A — PRODUCT DEFECT, filed as [rebar:7f93-2743-a597-4f98] (child of e369, priority 1,
`discovered_from` this ticket). The outbound path asks for `"In Progress"`, no transition is named
that, the transport raises `ValueError`, and `apply_handlers.record_backstop_failure` SOFT-FAILS it
into `bridge_alerts` and returns `soft_failed=True`. The pass exits 0 with no traceback and the
issue's status never changes. `test_outbound_mutation_round_trips[04-transition-status]` is
therefore reporting a REAL BUG, not a test problem — its assertion
(`fields.status.name is 'To Do'`, expected `'In Progress'`) is exactly right.
**It is a silent PARTIAL failure, which is the nastiest shape.** `Done` happens to be both a
transition name and a status name on this workflow, so `closed -> "Done"` works by coincidence
while `in_progress -> "In Progress"` does not. Some statuses sync and others silently do not.

CONSEQUENCE B — TEST DEFECT, mine, in the INBOUND cell. `_in_status` calls
`tr.transition_issue_by_name(key, "In Progress")` directly to set up the DC-side state, and hits
the same lookup miss — but in the test it surfaces as an uncaught `ValueError` during setup, so the
inbound cell never even reaches its oracle. The inbound path is NOT implicated by this failure and
remains untested for status; the cell must drive by an available TRANSITION name and assert the
destination the server itself declares.

THE CODEBASE ALREADY KNEW, WHICH IS THE GALLING PART. `test_create_get_update_transition_roundtrip`
passes precisely because it was written around this trap, and its comment states it outright: "A
transition's NAME is not its destination STATUS name: Jira's classic workflow offers 'Start
Progress' -> status 'In Progress' ... Asserting the status equals the transition name therefore
fails against a real instance. The transitions payload declares the destination in `to.name`." The
insight was recorded in a test and never propagated to the transport contract that needed it.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE ON CLOUD: DIG's workflow evidently names transitions after their destinations,
so the two spellings coincide and the bug cannot fire there. Same shape as every other finding in
this epic — a Cloud-shaped convention assumed to hold on a DC-shaped instance.

REMEDIATION SPLIT: the transport fix belongs to 7f93 (resolve against `to.name` as well as the
transition name, exact-name first, raise on an ambiguous destination). The inbound cell's setup fix
belongs to THIS ticket. They must land in that order, or the outbound cell stays red for a reason
the inbound fix cannot address.

=== TRIAGE: finding 7 (inbound assignee) — MY TEST IS WRONG, THE PRODUCT IS NOT. No bug to file. ===

The cell asserts `.assignee` on the local ticket EQUALS the id `ensure_identity_for("jira", "admin",
...)` returns. It got `'admin'` — the raw DC username — and I flagged that as "the inbound assignee
is stored verbatim rather than resolved through the identity registry". Checked in source before
filing anything, and that reading is wrong on two counts.

 1. **A bare string IS the designed local shape, on BOTH deployments.**
    `inbound_fields._assignee_matches` (`inbound_fields.py:102-112`) exists precisely because the
    two forms differ, and says so: "Jira returns `assignee` as
    `{accountId, displayName, emailAddress}`; local tickets store assignee as a bare string that
    may be an email". The permissive matcher was added because a mismatch here "reports a phantom
    `assignee` change on every pass". So Cloud stores a bare string too — DC storing `'admin'` is
    parity, not divergence.
 2. **The mint is ADDITIVE BY CONTRACT and explicitly does not touch this field.**
    `_ensure_inbound_assignee_identity` (`apply_inbound_records.py:83-135`) mints or reuses a GHOST
    identity keyed on the external id so a LATER OUTBOUND pass can key on it, and its docstring is
    unambiguous: "ADDITIVE + best-effort: this NEVER changes the human-readable name extraction and
    NEVER fails the inbound apply". It also already handles DC correctly — `for key in ("accountId",
    "name")`, Cloud's key first, DC's second, which is exactly the fix bug 5f48 landed.

**AND J11'S OWN PLAN SAID SO, WHICH I SHOULD HAVE HONOURED WHEN WRITING THE CELL.** Its AC reads:
"inbound DC assignee mutations MINT AN IDENTITY SUCCESSFULLY — asserted positively ... **THE
OBSERVABLE, since the identity is not a field on the ticket JSON.**" The plan explicitly told me
the identity is NOT on the ticket, and I wrote an oracle that reads it off the ticket anyway. The
certified plan was right and my implementation of it was not.

THE CORRECT ORACLE, which is what the AC actually asks for: after the inbound pass, assert the
identity EXISTS and carries the shared `jira` family — e.g. that resolving
`ensure_identity_for("jira", <dc_username>, ...)` returns an id that was already minted by the pass
rather than created by the assertion itself, and separately that `.assignee` is non-empty. The
distinction matters because `ensure_identity_for` is create-or-reuse: calling it and comparing to
its own return value can never fail, which is close to what my cell was doing. The fix must
establish "the PASS minted it" — e.g. by capturing the identity registry state before and after.

STATUS: this is a J11 test fix, in `test_dc_mutations.py`, NOT a product change and NOT a new bug.
Two of the seven findings are now resolved as test-side (this one and the inbound half of
transition-status); one is a real product defect already fixed ([rebar:7f93-2743-a597-4f98],
Gerrit 1202). Four remain: idempotence churn, inbound edit-summary, inbound link, inbound probe.

=== TRIAGE: finding 1 (idempotence / converged-pair churn) — ROOT CAUSE PROVEN, AND IT IS A
PRODUCT DEFECT. It is NOT in the outbound differ. ===

THE PLAN ENTRY IS NOT FROM `outbound_differ`. That was the wrong suspect, and the entry itself
says so. Run 30724309686 reported
`{'direction':'outbound','action':'update','target':'RBJQFTF-1','local_id':'RBJQFTF-1'}` — note
`local_id` IS THE JIRA KEY. An `outbound_differ` update carries
`provenance["local_id"] = om.local_id`, the LOCAL ticket id (`run_differs.py:562-566`), which
here would be `jira-rbjqftf-1`. Only ONE emitter in the codebase produces `local_id == target ==
<jira key>`: `differ._derive_provenance` (`differ.py:130-131`), whose last-resort fallback is
`local_id = target`. So the churn comes from the LEGACY SNAPSHOT DIFFER, not the field differ.

THE MECHANISM, end to end:

1. `run_differs.py:222` calls `ctx.differ.compute_mutations(ctx.prev_snapshot, ctx.curr_snapshot)`
   — it feeds the PREVIOUS PASS'S REMOTE SNAPSHOT into the parameter that differ.py's own module
   docstring (`differ.py:5-11`) defines as "the local source-of-truth state", and which it says
   REPLACED the legacy `compute_mutations(prev_snapshot, next_snapshot)` contract. Production is
   still calling it with the legacy argument.
2. `_compute_mutations_emit_both` (`differ.py:556-607`) then diffs every field not in
   `EXCLUDED_FIELDS = ("local_id","rebar-id")` (`config.py:5`) and, on any difference, emits
   `(outbound, update)` with `changed[field] = local_val` — i.e. the STALE prev-snapshot value.
   Read against the real arguments this means: any change to the Jira issue between two passes is
   emitted as an outbound update that would push the OLD value back.
3. `reconcile.py:613` advances the prev snapshot with `shutil.copy2(curr_path, prev_path)` — the
   PRE-APPLY fetch. So an outbound write applied during pass N is invisible to `prev` at pass N+1.
   The comment one line above (`reconcile.py:609`) states the intent it fails to meet: "Advance
   prev snapshot so the next call converges to zero mutations."
4. Therefore, one pass after OUR OWN outbound summary write lands, prev(old) vs curr(new) differ
   and the phantom is emitted. `persist` is False in a dry-run, so prev NEVER advances and the
   dry-run re-plans it forever. That is exactly what the cell reports.

REPRODUCED LOCALLY, NO JIRA NEEDED — byte-identical to the harness output:

    prev = {"RBJQFTF-1": {...,"summary": OLD, ...}}      # persisted pre-apply by pass N
    curr = {"RBJQFTF-1": {...,"summary": NEW, ...}}      # the fetch now sees our own write
    differ.compute_mutations(prev, curr)
    -> [{'direction':'outbound','action':'update','target':'RBJQFTF-1',
         'local_id':'RBJQFTF-1','payload':{'summary': OLD}}]

    control: compute_mutations(curr, curr) -> []

The payload is the OLD summary: the phantom proposes to REVERT the write the cell just made.

IT IS INERT AT APPLY TIME, WHICH IS WHY PRODUCTION NEVER NOTICED. The payload is a bare field
dict, not `{"changed_fields": ...}`, so `batch_dispatch._mutation_to_batch_dict:100-103` resolves
`fields = payload.get("changed_fields") or payload.get("fields", {})` to `{}` and
`dispatch_one._update_one_scalar_update:640-650` issues an empty `update_issue(key)`. Nothing
changes on the instance. So the mutation can never be "done" — it is planned every pass, counts
against the BOOTSTRAP_STRICT cap of 10 (`mode.py:104-111`), inflates `mutation_count`, and makes
"converged" a lie. Unconvergeable by construction. (Do NOT "fix" it by correcting the payload
shape: that would make it apply, and it would then revert every remote edit and flip-flop.)

ONE CAUSE EXPLAINS ALL THIRTEEN OF RUN 3's IDEMPOTENCE FAILURES, in both directions — the trigger
is "the DC issue changed since the last persisted fetch", regardless of which side changed it or
which field. inbound 05/06-label, 08/09-assignee, 03-description and outbound 02/03/05/07/08 all
fit without exception.

THIS IS A SIBLING OF AN ALREADY-CLOSED BUG, which settles the legitimacy question. `differ.py:80-92`
plus the label branch at `differ.py:576-582` were added by ticket robe-creek-zealot and describe
this exact mechanism verbatim: "The snapshot differ compares the PREVIOUS pass's Jira snapshot
against the current one, so our own label write-back from the prior pass surfaces here as apparent
remote drift one pass later — and emitted a spurious (outbound, update) echo". That fix was applied
to LABELS ONLY; every other field still churns. Same finding as the 9263 comment on this ticket:
on finding a defect class, sweep for siblings. Story 26de's contract is also explicit
(`differ.py:688-691`): "a write recorded as local-origin on pass N must not re-emit on pass N+1
even if the jira snapshot has not yet caught up."

THE SAME EMITTER ALSO EXPLAINS FINDING 6 (deleted issue plans no inbound probe). Its failure text
shows `{'direction':'outbound','action':'create','target':'RBJWUOX-1','local_id':'RBJWUOX-1'}` —
the same `local_id == target == key` signature. Deleting the issue drops it out of `curr`, and a
key present in prev-but-not-curr is read by this differ as "local has it, Jira does not" -> an
outbound CREATE proposing to RE-CREATE the issue we just deleted. Finding 6 should be triaged
against the same emitter rather than against the probe path.

REMEDIATION, filed separately as a bug under e369. The narrow fix is to stop the snapshot differ's
field-drift outbound updates from reaching the mutation list, at the `run_differs.py:222` call
site, and NOT to touch `differ.compute_mutations`'s documented local-vs-jira contract (its unit
tests legitimately exercise that contract with real local state). For a bound pair, field sync in
both directions is already owned by `_run_differs_outbound` / `_run_differs_inbound`, which run
immediately after; the snapshot differ's contribution there is pure noise. No J11 test change is
needed: the cell is correct and its diagnosis ("this is real churn") was right.

=== TRIAGE: the OUTBOUND transition-status cell — ROOT CAUSE PROVEN. It is a PRODUCT DEFECT,
and 7f93 does NOT cover it. Filed as [rebar:d067-5d2f-bcee-46ae]. ===

THE OUTBOUND PATH NEVER CALLS `transition_issue_by_name`, so 7f93's fix to that method cannot
reach it. 7f93 fixed the INBOUND cell because `_in_status` calls the transport method DIRECTLY.
The outbound cell goes somewhere else entirely, and that somewhere has no status handling on DC.

THE CHAIN, read end to end and cited:
 1. `adapters/jira_family/outbound_mapper.py:81-82` — the local `in_progress` becomes
    `fields["status"] = "In Progress"` via `LOCAL_STATUS_TO_JIRA` (`value_maps.py:49-57`).
 2. `dispatch_apply_phases.py:41` — `_OUTBOUND_BATCH_ALLOWLIST` CONTAINS `"status"`, so
    `_update_one_filter_fields` (`:130-139`) KEEPS it rather than stripping it.
 3. `dispatch_one.py:665` — `_update_one_scalar_update` forwards the whole allowlisted dict as
    `client.update_issue(issue_key, **fields)`.
 4. `applier.py:591` — that `client` is `_load_acli()`, which is
    `select_backend(load_config()).transport` (`applier.py:221-231`). On this deployment,
    `JiraDataCenterTransport`.
 5. **THE FORK.** On Cloud, `adapters/jira/acli.py:170` POPS `status` out of the kwargs and
    `:182-183` routes it to `transition_issue` -> `transition_issue_by_name`. The
    status→transition translation lives IN THE TRANSPORT, once, per vendor.
    On Data Center, `adapters/jira_datacenter/transport.py:248-255` pops ONLY `assignee` and
    puts everything else into `issue.update(fields=kwargs)` — a REST field EDIT. `status` is

## The 7 missing mutation cells are now written (Gerrit 1251, 1252, 1253)

The completion gate's finding was correct and this closes it structurally. Seven
cells added to tests/external/live_jira_dc/test_dc_mutations.py, one per missing
table position. Collected count for that module goes 23 -> 30; for the whole
live_jira_dc directory 49 -> 56, i.e. +7 exactly, no other cell disturbed.

### What went where, and why

ALL SEVEN are standalone rather than _INBOUND_CELLS / _OUTBOUND_CELLS rows. That
is not a shortcut in any of the seven; each has a structural reason:

- rows 9, 11 (both directions), 13 (both directions) all need a CONVERGED prior
  state before the mutation under test (an assign before a clear, an add before a
  removal, a parent before a detach). The table driver runs exactly ONE pass per
  row, so a two-pass cell cannot be a row. This is the same reason row 6
  (remove label) was already standalone.
- rows 12 and 13 additionally need a SUB-TASK, and the driver hands every row the
  bound_dc_issue fixture, which is a Task. On Data Center only a sub-task has a
  fields.parent at all (transport.py:645-690).
- row 14 outbound has no pass-level emitter to route through: no differ emits an
  (outbound, delete), the only production callers of delete_issue are the create
  rollback (apply_outbound.py:100-113) and the typed leaf (:168-183), and rebar
  has no local ticket deletion to diff against. ADR 0028 section 1 forbids
  driving a destructive action from absence, which is what row 14 INBOUND asserts.

The cells, by row:

| row | direction | test | oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | inbound | test_inbound_delete_link_round_trips | the local dep no longer targets the counterpart |
| 12 | inbound | test_inbound_set_subtask_parent_round_trips | .parent_id equals the SECOND parent's local id |
| 13 | inbound | test_inbound_clear_parent_round_trips | .parent_id is empty |
| 9 | outbound | test_outbound_unassign_round_trips | fields.assignee is empty on the instance |
| 11 | outbound | test_outbound_delete_link_round_trips | fields.issuelinks no longer names the counterpart |
| 13 | outbound | test_outbound_clear_parent_round_trips | fields.parent is absent |
| 14 | outbound | test_outbound_delete_leaves_the_issue_absent_by_key_AND_by_id | HTTP 404 by key AND by numeric id |

### How each clear/delete cell asserts ABSENCE positively

None of them assert "no exception was raised" — that is worthless here, the whole
d067 defect was a soft-failed error with exit 0.

- delete link, both directions: the counterpart key is ABSENT from the read-back
  link set, after the ADD was asserted to have landed first (so absence cannot be
  inherited).
- clear assignee: fields.assignee read back off the instance is falsy, after the
  ASSIGN was asserted to have landed. This also catches the worse failure mode
  (an empty-string user search that MATCHES someone, leaving the issue assigned
  to an arbitrary account) which an "is it still admin?" check would miss.
- clear parent, both directions: fields.parent / .parent_id is falsy, after the
  parent was asserted PRESENT on the relevant side first.
- delete ticket: HTTP 404 from raw REST by BOTH handles, after HTTP 200 by both
  handles was asserted BEFORE the delete. The by-id half is bug 7c26's pair: a
  MOVED issue is re-keyed and its old key 404s exactly like a deleted one, so a
  key-only check would report "deleted" for a live issue.

Every wait in the new cells is on the PRODUCTION read path, not a direct GET:
get_issuelinks_map (what fetcher.py:592 calls) and get_parent_map (what
fetcher.py:485-511 calls). Both are index-backed, so waiting on the immediately
consistent direct GET would let index lag be reported as a bridge defect.

### The two docstrings that overclaimed are fixed, and the fix is a SPLIT

test_inbound_link_round_trips and test_outbound_link_round_trips each said
"Rows 10-11" while asserting only the add; the outbound one went further and
claimed "Both halves in one cell because the removal is only meaningful after the
add has been PROVEN to land" when there was no removal in the body at all. Both
are now scoped to row 10 and say explicitly what they were narrowed from, and the
removals are their own cells doing exactly what the old text described. Splitting
rather than appending is deliberate: a removal can fail for reasons an add cannot,
and bundling them makes one red report two indistinguishable things (the lesson
change 1188 paid for). NO existing assertion was weakened or deleted.

### Three PRODUCT defects found, filed, not fixed

Writing these cells proved three defects by code path. Per this story's rule the
cells assert the AC's oracle, not the current behaviour, so they are EXPECTED RED
until the product is fixed. Do not invert them to make CI green — that would
freeze the gaps.

1. [rebar:751e-06f1-bb0b-464c] DC outbound clear-assignee never unassigns. An
   empty local assignee resolves to the EMPTY STRING (outbound_differ.py:504-505),
   which the DC transport forwards verbatim to assign_issue (transport.py:281-303,
   no empty-value branch), and pycontribs 3.10.5 treats only None / -1 / "-1" as
   Unassigned (JIRA._get_user_id). Cloud has the fix and DC never got its half:
   acli.py:342-345,357-359 routes empty through unassign_issue precisely because
   passing it on silently no-ops (bug 85a1). Same Cloud-has-it/DC-doesn't shape as
   bug d067.
2. [rebar:2b16-9be0-a8f5-41d9] Inbound link removal is never mirrored.
   inbound_differ._diff_links_inbound is ADD-only by construction and by its own
   docstring (inbound_differ.py:380 and :396). The OUTBOUND direction does have a
   removal path (outbound_links.py:120-175), so this is an asymmetry, not a
   whole-feature omission.
3. [rebar:88d9-fe42-e50f-4067] Inbound parent clear is never emitted. Two layers
   independently drop the signal: the fetcher leaves the parent field ABSENT when
   the mapped parent is None (fetcher.py:508-511), and the differ explicitly
   refuses to emit parent_id=None (inbound_differ.py:266-270). The apply layer is
   already ready for the clear (apply_inbound_records.py:361-372).

All three are linked discovered_from this story.

### Verification done, and what is deferred to CI

The harness CANNOT run on this host (linux/amd64 image, stalls under arm64
emulation — README.md:53-67), so validation here is structural:

- REBAR_RUN_EXTERNAL=1 pytest tests/external/live_jira_dc --collect-only: 49 -> 56.
- tests/unit/test_external_isolation.py: passes. Every new cell carries both the
  harness skipif and the extra skipif, so none of them burns the session budget
  harness-free.
- _live_jira_ready is untouched at module level, so this module stays in the
  all-skip canary's bookkeeping (the rule change 1203 had to repair).
- ruff check + ruff format + mypy: clean (the commit gate ran all three).
- The two local-side primitives the new cells depend on were probed against a
  throwaway store rather than assumed: edit_ticket(assignee="") leaves .assignee
  as "", and clearing a parent requires --parent=null (an empty value is rejected
  outright with "use --parent=null to detach").
- The sub-task issue type is DISCOVERED from the instance, not hardcoded, for the
  reason conftest._discover_project_templates records about template keys.

### Module size

test_dc_mutations.py: 1065 -> 1767 lines. The 800-LOC hard cap is scoped to
src/rebar/**/*.py in BOTH enforcers (.github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml
"Absolute cap: no src/rebar/**/*.py file may exceed the limit" and
tests/unit/test_module_size_contract.py, which rglobs src_root only), so this file
is not gated and was already over 800 before this change. NOT split: splitting a
live-suite module risks dropping it from the _live_jira_ready canary, which is
exactly the failure change 1203 existed to repair.

### Known remaining gap, NOT in the gate's list of 7

Row 12 OUTBOUND's sub-task case is still only implicitly covered: the epic case is
asserted directly (test_set_parent_declines_the_epic_case_loudly) and the new
row-13 outbound cell asserts a sub-task parent is present as its SETUP, but that
parent came from issue creation rather than from a rebar push. Recording it here
rather than silently widening scope.

## INDEPENDENT AC VERIFICATION (all 18) — 15 supportable, criterion 11 NOT TICKABLE AS WRITTEN, and
## ONE LIVE CELL FOUND THAT CANNOT FAIL

Commissioned a read-only pass over all 18 criteria against the LANDED tree rather than against this
ticket's own summaries of itself, because ticking a box asserts the item is done. Evidence base: the
worktree tree plus the last recorded harness run 30772461871 (`main @ bd3de0f864`, 48 passed / 1 failed,
canary `collected=49 executed=49 skipped=0`). **That run predates the seven newest cells — the live
suite now collects 56, so SEVEN CELLS HAVE NEVER EXECUTED AGAINST THE HARNESS.** No live cell was run
during verification (arm64 host; the harness is amd64-only).

### The finding that matters most: inbound cell `08-assign` CANNOT FAIL — both halves are vacuous

`_in_assign` (test_dc_mutations.py:311-320) assigns `ADMIN_USER`; `_oracle_in_assign` (:323-334) asserts
only that `.assignee` is TRUTHY. But `bound_dc_issue`'s seeded issue arrives **already assigned to the
project lead (admin)** — this suite asserts that itself in two places (`_dc_support.py:204-212` and
`test_dc_mutations.py:1517-1526`), and harness run 30763838558 demonstrated it by finding `jira/'admin'`
already mapped. So the mutation is a NO-OP and the oracle checks a field the binding pass had already
populated. The cell passes whether or not inbound assignee sync works at all.

This is this epic's signature failure class, found inside the very suite whose purpose is to end it —
the same shape as the vacuous assignee oracle that, once repaired, immediately surfaced real defect
8d68 after months of green. The AC's row-8 inbound oracle is "`.assignee` is the mapped identity"; a
truthiness check is not that. **Being repaired** (see the remediation note below), using the pattern the
MINT cell already established at :1466-1586 — establish ABSENCE first (`forget_identity_mapping` +
assert `resolve_mapping(...) is None`), then assert the SPECIFIC mapped identity.

### Criterion 11 ("all 14 mutations x 2 directions") — NOT TICKABLE AS WRITTEN. Three deviations.

26 of the 28 named cells exist and were individually enumerated. The gaps:

 1. **ROW 1 OUTBOUND IS ENTIRELY MISSING** — and it was NOT on this ticket's own list of known gaps.
    The criterion requires asserting the DC issue carries the provenance label `rebar-id:<local_id>`
    AND the entity property `local_id` read by raw REST.
    `grep -rn "rebar-id:\|properties/local_id" tests/external/` returns NOTHING. **Being added.**
 2. **ROW 12 OUTBOUND (sub-task) is only implicit** — already self-recorded in comment 29: the parent

 3. **ROW 14 INBOUND asserts a DIFFERENT oracle than the AC text, for a verified-correct reason.** The

    == 1`. The code (:1340-1395) instead asserts "no teardown entry, and the local ticket survives".

    ticking, because an AC that prescribes a MECHANISM can be wrong about the mechanism — the same

* **SUB-TASK child → SUPPORTED.** `jira_datacenter/transport.py` `set_parent` (:668-712) checks

So the sub-task case is a genuine round-trip and the criterion needed a cell, not an amendment.

### THE NEW FINDING — a pass-level round-trip is STRUCTURALLY UNREACHABLE on DC

`outbound_field_diff._resolve_local_parent:136-139` omits the parent field ENTIRELY unless the parent's
local `ticket_type` is `epic` (bug 8b25's hierarchy guard, over `local_ticket_types` at
`outbound_differ.py:475-477`, unit-covered by `conflict/test_parent_hierarchy_guard.py`). A DC sub-task's
parent is a STANDARD issue, which imports as local `ticket_type` `"task"`.

**The emit gate wants an epic parent; the apply gate wants a sub-task child. On DC those sets are
DISJOINT** — so no reconcile pass can emit an outbound parent-set DC would accept. Each gate is defensible
alone; both were written for Cloud's next-gen hierarchy and nobody composed them against DC's model.

Filed as **[rebar:39c1-2a32-b564-4b4b]** (linked `discovered_from` here) — a PRODUCT gap, not a test gap,
and the FIFTH instance of "Cloud has the translation, DC never got its half" after d067, 8d68, 751e, and
2b16/88d9. It is recorded as NOT gating e369, consistent with the operator's e39f ruling, and the ticket
flags plainly that this is a BORDERLINE call because — unlike e39f — it does not fail safe.

### The cell shape, and why it is not a weakened oracle

Transport-level round-trip, following `test_outbound_delete_leaves_the_issue_absent_by_key_AND_by_id`
(row 14 outbound), which asserts its primitive for exactly this reason and says so: routing it through a
pass would mean asserting a mutation nothing emits. It seeds parents A and B plus a sub-task under A,
asserts the STARTING parent is A, calls `set_parent(child, B)`, then reads
`GET /rest/api/2/issue/{child}?fields=parent` over **raw REST** and asserts `fields.parent.key == B`.
Still a real round-trip — rebar writes, the instance is read back independently — merely scoped to the
layer that can run. The swallow at `dispatch_one.py:571-578` never enters the picture because the
transport is called directly.

Raw REST was chosen over the two alternatives BECAUSE they would have weakened it: `get_issue_by_rest`
goes through the same transport that wrote (cannot separate "DC stored it" from "the object we mutated
reports what we set"), and `get_parent_map` is an eventually-consistent JQL paged search that the INBOUND
row already owns.

**No cell was added asserting the differ suppression as correct behaviour** — that would freeze the gap
into the suite, which this module warns against elsewhere.

Nothing under `tests/unit/` exercised DC `set_parent` at all before this. Driven with a fake pycontribs
client: a sub-task produces exactly `[{"parent": {"key": "RBJ-2"}}]`; a non-sub-task raises
`NotImplementedError` naming both "sub-task" and "Epic Link" **and issues no write**. The disjoint gates
are asserted BOTH ways, so if the emit gate ever changes, that test tells the next reader to re-shape this
cell as a full round-trip.

    the outbound parent set: fields.parent on RBJ-3 is STILL 'RBJ-1' — the parent it had BEFORE the
    mutation. Expected 'RBJ-2'. This is the silent-no-op signature: `set_parent` writes `fields.parent`

and HTTP 404 (`not readable by raw REST`). GREEN on `parent.key == 'RBJ-2'` with `previous_parent='RBJ-1'`.

The live cell has never run (arm64 host). What is proven is that the oracle discriminates and that the
transport's two branches behave as claimed — both now executable against a fake client. Corroboration
that the primitive works on the real harness is INDIRECT but real: `test_inbound_set_subtask_parent_round_trips`

Criterion 11's oracle table specifies, for row 12 outbound:

> sub-task case: `fields.parent`; EPIC case: NOT round-tripped — `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)`
> against the transport

and the criterion defends that carve-out at length: routing it through the reconciler "would make it
untestable by construction, because `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` and
only logs".

**That reasoning was sound and the prescription is now wrong**, for a reason outside this ticket:
[rebar:39c1-2a32-b564-4b4b] set out to make the epic case WORK, and change **1311** implements it as
a write to the instance-discovered "Epic Link" custom field. An AC that requires the epic case to

The live cell has accordingly been rewritten from `test_set_parent_declines_the_epic_case_loudly` to

`set_parent` does with an epic parent, and never let `fields.parent` be written where DC no-ops it),
different expected outcome.

 * The carve-out's ORIGINAL justification still holds and is preserved. The new cell also asserts
   **directly against the transport plus a raw-REST read-back**, NOT through a reconcile pass —
   precisely because `dispatch_one` still swallows the exception, so a pass-level assertion would
   still be untestable by construction. Only the expected outcome changed; the observability
   argument the AC makes is unchanged and is the reason the cell is shaped the way it is.

   Epic, performs the write, reads the field back over raw REST, then clears it and asserts the

applied unilaterally, since 5200's criterion 11 has already been the subject of one ruling):

    | 12 | set parent | `.parent_id` is the parent's local id | sub-task case: `fields.parent`;

# J11 — Prove bidirectional reconciliation live, against a realistic store

## Why this exists

Epic e369's headline AC is:

> [operator-attested] rebar reconciles bidirectionally against the Dockerized Jira instance ... at
> least one issue created in DC appears in the local store after an inbound pass, and one local edit
> appears on the DC issue after an outbound pass, with zero unhandled exceptions

It is NOT met, and the way it failed is instructive. CI run 30637886718 reported:

    invariants: scanned=0 filed=0
    OK: steady-state pass converged
    RECON: outbound_differ total=0   inbound_differ total=0

**Scanned zero.** The pass converged because there was nothing to reconcile. That proves the
reconciler runs cleanly against an EMPTY instance — it does not prove data moves. On an empty store
'converged' and 'works' are indistinguishable, and only one of them is the criterion. Closing the epic
on that output would have been the fifth instance in this epic of green-but-broken.

The existing live module builds its store with the `rebar_repo` fixture: `rebar.init_repo()` on an
empty temp dir. Nothing to sync, so nothing syncs.

## Approach

Run the live verification against a COPY OF THIS PROJECT'S ACTUAL TICKET STORE, so the pass sees
realistic volume, ticket shapes, link graphs, comment histories and field values — the conditions that
surface ordering and field-mapping defects an empty store cannot.
(Deliberately NOT "pagination": that is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of the local store,
and is exercised by seeding the harness — see the volume bullet below. An earlier draft listed it here
and contradicted that bullet.)

### Isolation is the first requirement, not an afterthought

rebar AUTO-COMMITS and AUTO-PUSHES ticket events to `sync.remote`. A copy of this project's store that
retained its configuration could push test mutations back at the real project. Defence in depth, in
priority order:

1. **A SEPARATE REPO WITH NO REMOTES — the primary mechanism.** The CI job `git init`s a fresh repo
   and copies the ticket-store content in. It never adds `origin`, so there is physically
   nowhere to push, independent of any config or env value. This is stronger than a flag
   because it cannot be defeated by a mis-read setting.
   **HOW the content is obtained, because it is NOT in a normal checkout:** `.tickets-tracker/` is
   GITIGNORED (`.gitignore:9`) and the store lives on the ORPHAN `tickets` branch, which
   `actions/checkout` does not fetch. The job must explicitly `git fetch origin tickets` in the
   SOURCE checkout and materialise that tree, then `git init` + commit it in the destination.
   Copying the workspace directory would copy nothing.
   **EXTRACT INTO `.tickets-tracker/`, NOT INTO THE REPO ROOT — an earlier draft's command was
   wrong and would have produced a store the reconciler cannot see.** The orphan `tickets` branch
   holds the ticket files AND `.bridge_state` at ITS OWN ROOT (`git ls-tree origin/tickets` shows
   `.bridge_state`, `.store-compat.json`, and bare ticket-id entries such as `003a-09ae-9983-4007`),
   whereas the reconciler reads `tracker_dir = repo_root / ".tickets-tracker"` (`reconcile.py:265`).
   Extracting to the root therefore lands every ticket one directory ABOVE where the pass looks,
   so the pass sees NO LOCAL TICKETS — a store that is empty as far as the reconciler is
   concerned, reproduced by the setup rather than by the product. (Note this does NOT surface as
   `scanned=0`: that number counts REMOTE Jira issues, not local tickets — see the store-copy AC.
   It is caught by the ticket-count check, which is why that check reads the filesystem.)
   The command is:
       mkdir -p <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
       git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
   and the fixture must ASSERT the layout after extraction (ticket files exist under
   `.tickets-tracker/`) rather than trust the redirection.
   **THE WORKING REPO ALSO NEEDS A CONFIG, and it has none — it is a fresh `git init`.** The copied
   tree carries tickets, not reconciler settings, so the fixture must WRITE a `rebar.toml` into the
   fresh repo containing `[reconciler]` with `base_url = "http://localhost:2990/jira"` (plus the
   project key and `allow_insecure = true`, since the harness serves plain http). That written file is
   also what the `base_url` AC below inspects — the check and the setup must name the same file, or
   the check passes by finding nothing.
2. `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` as a second, independent layer (`sync.push` accepts `always|async|off`;
   the env override is authoritative).
   **Do NOT assert on `sync.remote`.** It defaults to `"origin"` (`_config_schema.py:307`) whether or
   not such a remote exists, so "sync.remote is empty" is neither achievable nor meaningful — and
   setting it empty to satisfy a check would give false confidence while changing nothing. The
   assertion that carries real weight is that `git remote` in the working repo returns NOTHING.
3. The reconciler config points ONLY at the harness (`reconciler.base_url` = the container). No Cloud
   credentials are present in the job environment at all — no `JIRA_URL`, no `JIRA_API_TOKEN`, no
   `acli` auth — so the Cloud path cannot be driven even by accident.
4. **The isolation is ASSERTED, not assumed.** A test fails the job if `git remote` returns anything in
   the working repo. (NOT on `sync.remote` — see layer 2: it defaults to `"origin"` regardless, so
   that assertion can never pass and would only invite someone to weaken it.) Safety that is not
   tested is an intention.

### The copy must be SCRUBBED of Jira IDs and reconciler artifacts

Isolation stops ticket events ESCAPING. It does not stop the reconciler forming an intent to WRITE to
a production issue key. The scrub is an independent layer and both are required.

Enumerated against this project's REAL tickets branch, not assumed:

    .bridge_state/bindings.json
    .bridge_state/bindings-retired.json
    .bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/bindings.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/prev_snapshot.json

Two traps a naive scrub falls into:

* **`.bridge_state.bak-retarget/` also holds real bindings.** It is a backup left by a past project
  retarget. Deleting `.bridge_state/` by name removes the live set and leaves a SECOND full set of
  production Jira bindings in the copy. Match the pattern `.bridge_state*`, and assert none survive —
  do not delete a hardcoded list. The existence of this directory is itself proof that the artifact
  set drifts over time, so the scrub must ENUMERATE the copied tree.
* **`prev_snapshot.json` must still be scrubbed — but it is NOT detectable from mutation counts,
  and two earlier drafts of this plan got that wrong in opposite directions.** It is the OUTBOUND
  field-change baseline (`OutboundDiffConfig.prev_snapshot`, consumed in
  `outbound_differ.compute_outbound_mutations`), NOT an inbound create/delete trigger: the inbound
  and legacy differs decide creates from the CURRENT snapshot. So a leftover production copy does
  not drive mass DELETION — that much an earlier draft got right.
  What that draft then got WRONG is the claim that it produces a wave of spurious outbound UPDATEs
  that the run can detect. It cannot, and the reason is mechanical: `outbound_differ.py:518-520`
  branches on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`, and `None` routes to the CREATE path — an
  UPDATE is only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`,
  so no ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` surviving ON ITS OWN emits nothing at all.
  **Therefore it is caught DIRECTLY, by the scrub-completeness criterion asserting `.bridge_state*`
  is absent — an observation of the file itself, not an inference from mutation counts.** See the
  zero-counts AC for the full derivation; this bullet and that AC must agree, and an earlier
  revision left them contradicting each other.

### The DC-side mutation suite

Comprehensive mutations applied to the HARNESS instance (never a real Jira), each asserted to
round-trip against a NAMED per-mutation oracle (the table in the acceptance criteria gives the
proving read for every cell), so the bridge is exercised rather than merely started. The ONE
exception is `set_parent`'s epic case, which by design does not round-trip and is asserted
directly against the transport — stated here as well as in the ACs so the two cannot drift:

* **inbound (DC -> local), fourteen mutations:** create issue; edit summary; edit description;
  transition status; add label; remove label; add comment; assign; unassign; create issue link;
  delete issue link; set sub-task parent; clear parent; delete issue (absence probe).
  **`edit comment` is deliberately NOT in this list.** An earlier draft required it in both
  directions. The reconciler has no edit-comment mutation type and `JiraDataCenterTransport` has no
  `update_comment`, so it specified a capability that does not exist. If comment editing is wanted it
  is a separate feature story, not a verification criterion.
* **outbound (local -> DC), enumerated rather than described as "the mirror set":** create ticket ->
  issue; edit title -> summary; edit description; transition status; add label; remove label; add
  comment; set assignee; clear assignee; create link; delete link; set parent; clear parent; delete
  ticket. Fourteen, matching the inbound list one-for-one — `set_parent`'s epic case is expected to
  raise `NotImplementedError` (see bda8's triage), asserted **directly against the transport**
  (`with pytest.raises(NotImplementedError): transport.set_parent(...)`), NOT through the reconciler
  subprocess. `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` (dispatch_one.py:564) and
  only logs, so the exception is SWALLOWED inside a pass: no traceback, unchanged return code, and
  therefore indistinguishable on the subprocess streams from a mutation that succeeded. Routing that
  assertion through the subprocess would make it untestable by construction — the same
  swallowed-exception trap that let J9's twelve missing members pass 1600 tests.
* **volume — and note WHAT drives it.** Pagination is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of
  the local store copy. The store copy buys realistic local volume, ticket shapes and link graphs;
  it does NOT exercise paging at all. To exercise paging the suite must CREATE issues in the harness.
  Procedure, because guessing the cap is how truncation stays hidden: first READ the instance's
  effective page size (issue a `search_issues` with a high `maxResults` and observe what the server
  actually returns — Jira 8.17.1 defaults to 50, but `jira.search.views.default.max` is
  server-configurable and the server silently truncates), then seed at least `2 * observed + 1`
  issues so at least three pages are required. Assert the observed cap in the test output so a
  future instance change is visible rather than silent.
* **idempotence:** an immediately repeated pass after each direction writes nothing.

### Sequence: a thin slice BEFORE the comprehensive suite

The riskiest unknown is not any individual mutation — it is whether the copied-and-scrubbed store
drives a live pass at all. So land a vertical slice first: fetch + scrub + isolation assertions, ONE
inbound round-trip (create in DC, assert it appears locally) and ONE outbound round-trip (edit
locally, assert it appears in DC). Only once that is green in CI does the full mutation suite go in.
Building all thirteen mutations against an unproven harness path risks debugging thirteen failures
that share one root cause.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` — the `jira-dc-harness` job gains the store-copy step
  (fresh `git init`, no remote) and the isolation assertions.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/` — the mutation suite and its fixtures; a `dc_mutations` helper that
  applies each DC-side change through the real transport.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/README.md` — document the isolation contract and WHY (auto-push).

**NOT in scope:** any change that could write to this project's Jira or its tickets branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] the working repo in CI has NO git remote, asserted by a test that FAILS the job otherwise —
      this is the primary isolation and it must be verified, not assumed
- [ ] `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` is asserted in the same test as the no-remote check
- [ ] no Cloud credential is present in the job environment, asserted by test
- [ ] the store under test is a COPY of this project's real ticket store, proved by COUNTING
      LOCAL TICKETS DIRECTLY — not by the pass's `scanned` number.
      **THIS AC PREVIOUSLY MEASURED THE WRONG SIDE OF THE BRIDGE, and correcting it also corrects
      this epic's founding diagnosis.** `scanned` is `len(curr_snapshot)` (`run_differs.py:282`),
      and `curr_snapshot` is `fetcher.compute_snapshot(...)` (`reconcile.py:286`) — the normalized
      **JIRA** snapshot, i.e. the count of REMOTE issues fetched from the harness. It says nothing
      whatever about how many LOCAL tickets the copied store holds. The isolated harness starts
      with no issues, so a pass run before any DC seeding reports zero no matter how large the copy
      is; the old AC would have failed on a perfectly good store, and could never have proved the
      thing it was written to prove.
      This also means the epic's original reading of the earlier failing run was wrong. That run's
      `scanned=0` was recorded (handoff #4) as "it converged because the STORE was EMPTY". On this
      code it means the HARNESS had no issues — a remote-side fact. The local store may well have
      been fine. The conclusion drawn from it (that a pass over an empty input proves nothing)
      still stands; the mechanism attributed to it does not.
      **THE CORRECT OBSERVABLE — count the copy, on the filesystem, before any pass runs.** Assert
      that the number of ticket entries under `<working repo>/.tickets-tracker/` equals the number
      on the fetched `tickets` branch (`git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD`, excluding the dot-files
      `.bridge_state*`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitignore`, `.store-compat.json`, `.ticket-write.lock`),
      and that it is > 0. Comparing the two counts rather than asserting a bare floor is what makes
      this catch a PARTIAL extraction, which a `> 0` check would wave through.
      Keep the remote-side number too, but label it honestly: after the pagination cells seed the
      harness, the same line reports how many issues the fetch actually saw, and that is the
      truncation signal the seeding criterion already owns. Where to read it, since it is not in the
      JSON envelope and two earlier revisions of this AC got the stream and the wording wrong:
      `run_differs.py:270-283` branches on
      `skip_invariant_filing = (not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`:
        * DRY-RUN takes the SKIP branch — `persist` is False because `MODE_CAPS[DRY_RUN] == 0`
          (`reconcile.py:218-222`) — and prints to STDERR (so no-write mode keeps STDOUT a pure
          JSON payload):
              invariants: skipped (no-write mode, <N> issues in snapshot)
          There is NO `scanned=` line in this mode at all.
        * A FILTERED pass — what the mutation cells use — hits the SAME skip branch (the gate is
          `(not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`) and prints
          `invariants: skipped (filtered pass, <N> issues in snapshot)` to STDERR.
        * The `scanned=<N> filed=<M> (cap=5)` line on STDOUT is emitted ONLY by an UNFILTERED
          WRITING pass — which this plan never runs (see the scoping note: unfiltered passes are
          dry-run only). It is documented here so a future reader does not go looking for that
          line in this suite's output and conclude something is broken when it is simply absent.
      Do not read `.scanned` from the envelope; there is no such key. The sibling `filed` counts
      INVARIANT-VIOLATION tickets, not tickets filed from DC issues, so `filed=0` is not evidence
      about inbound either way.
- [ ] the scrub matches `.bridge_state*` as a GLOB and a test asserts ZERO binding or snapshot
      artifacts survive anywhere in the copied tree — derived by enumerating the tree, not from a
      hardcoded list
- [ ] a test asserts the `.bridge_state*` scrub is COMPLETE — nothing matching `.bridge_state*`
      survives anywhere under the copied tracker dir, so a partially-scrubbed tree fails the job.
      NOT "the copied store holds no production Jira key reference", which an earlier draft required
      and which is MECHANICALLY UNACHIEVABLE: ticket event files under `.tickets-tracker/`
      legitimately embed `jira_key` values from prior Cloud syncs, the scrub correctly leaves that
      historical data intact (only BINDINGS drive remote writes — `binding_store.py:113`), so a
      whole-tree scan for production keys would ALWAYS hit and could never pass
- [ ] the first pass plans EXACTLY ZERO deletion mutations AND EXACTLY ZERO outbound UPDATE
      mutations, both read from the `--mode dry-run` JSON envelope on stdout (the no-write branch at
      `__main__.py:445-452` is the one that emits JSON; writing modes emit only an `OK:` line, so
      dry-run is what makes these counts observable at all).
      **THE EXACT KEYS, so the assertion needs no guesswork.** The envelope is the whole result
      dict (`reconcile.py:690-709`). The per-mutation plan is the top-level `plan` array, built by
      `_build_plan_entries` (`reconcile_helpers.py:450-480`), whose entries are exactly
      `{direction, action, target, local_id}`. `direction` is `MutationDirection` (`"inbound"` |
      `"outbound"`) and `action` is `MutationAction` (`"create"` | `"update"` | `"delete"` |
      `"probe"` | `"clean_label"` | `"repair_property"` | `"conflict"`) — both `StrEnum`, so they
      serialize as those literal strings (`mutation.py:17-29`). The two assertions are therefore:
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.action == "delete")] | length == 0'
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "outbound" and .action == "update")] | length == 0'
      Read the envelope from STDOUT ONLY: the human-readable `OK: dry-run computed …` line goes to
      STDERR precisely so it cannot corrupt the JSON, so the test must not merge the two streams.
      **BOTH COUNTS ARE ZERO, and an earlier draft's rationale for a non-zero tolerance was
      MECHANICALLY WRONG — corrected here from the code rather than softened.** That draft said
      `< 10` outbound UPDATEs independently detects a surviving `prev_snapshot.json` while the
      deletion count stays at a reassuring zero. It cannot. `outbound_differ.py:518-520` branches
      on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`: `None` routes to the CREATE path, so an UPDATE is
      only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`, so no
      ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` that survives on its own produces NO outbound
      updates whatsoever — the assertion it was supposed to catch that failure with is blind to it.
      What the two assertions actually do:
        * ZERO deletions catches a surviving `bindings.json` — its production keys do not exist in
          the harness, so every bound ticket looks remotely deleted. This is the load-bearing one.
        * ZERO outbound updates is a SUBORDINATE guard on the same failure, for the case where a
          surviving binding's key happens to resolve in the harness. It is not an independent
          detector and must not be described as one.
      A surviving `prev_snapshot.json` is caught DIRECTLY instead, by the scrub-completeness
      criterion that asserts `.bridge_state*` is absent — an observation of the file, not an
      inference from mutation counts. Both counts are therefore exactly 0: with no bindings there
      is no legitimate source of either, and any non-zero value means the scrub failed.
- [ ] [operator-attested] an issue created in DC appears in the local store after an inbound pass.
      **The oracle for this is already FIXED and PROVEN, which an earlier draft did not record.**
      [rebar:23ed-de0a-765b-49aa] is CLOSED: the test had grepped the RAW Jira key against a payload
      whose id is the lowercased `jira-<key>` form and which carries no raw key at all, so it could
      never pass. It now matches by exact id via `_jira_key_to_local_id(remote_key)` AND asserts the
      binding store. EVIDENCE: CI run 30662366152, job "jira DC harness smoke",
      `test_a_dc_created_ticket_carries_the_shared_jira_provenance` PASSED in a fully green
      17-passed/0-skipped run. So this criterion is satisfiable today; it is the OUTBOUND half below
      that still has no evidence
- [ ] [operator-attested] a local edit appears on the DC issue after an outbound pass.
      THIS is the epic's unproven half and the reason this story exists: `test_reconcile_pass.py`
      has three live tests and NONE mutates a local ticket then asserts the change surfaces on the
      DC issue
- [ ] inbound DC assignee mutations MINT AN IDENTITY SUCCESSFULLY — asserted positively (the
      identity exists and carries the jira family), NOT merely that no exception escaped.
      **THE OBSERVABLE, since the identity is not a field on the ticket JSON.** After the inbound
      pass, call `rebar.ensure_identity_for("jira", <dc_user_name>, <display_name>)` — it is
      documented idempotent (resolve-or-mint, reusing an existing mapping) — and assert BOTH:
        (a) the id it returns EQUALS the local ticket's `.assignee` from `rebar show`, which is
            what proves the pass itself minted and attached the identity rather than the test
            creating one after the fact; and
        (b) the provider argument that satisfies (a) is the FAMILY string `"jira"`, not the
            deployment string `"jira-datacenter"` — that distinction IS bug 5f48, whose fix
            routes through `_identity_provider_for` asking the backend for `identity_family`
            (`apply_inbound_records.py:50-80`), because the store vocabulary is per-family.
      Assert on `<dc_user_name>` (Jira DC's `name`), not `accountId`: DC has no accountId at all,
      and the accountId-only guard is precisely what made 5f48 silent.
      **WHICH USER, resolved at runtime rather than hardcoded.** Take the assignee from
      `GET /rest/api/2/myself` on the harness — it returns the authenticated account's `name` and
      `displayName`, which are exactly the two values the assertion needs, and it cannot drift
      from whatever account the harness actually provisions (the compose default is `admin`, but
      reading it is what keeps this cell correct if that changes). Assign to that user and assert
      against the same pair.
      [rebar:5f48-244c-7063-42d0] is CLOSED and its fix is on `main` in commit 36e134401 ("b4e3:
      mint DC inbound identities as jira family", whose message records "Folds in bug 5f48"): the
      guard reads `for key in ("accountId", "name")` and `_identity_provider_for` asks the backend
      for `identity_family`. It was a SILENT failure — a swallowed `ValueError` degrading assignee
      resolution on every DC pass — and a no-exception assertion would have passed throughout it,
      which is exactly why this AC must assert the positive outcome
- [ ] every mutation in the suite above round-trips and is asserted INDIVIDUALLY (never by an
      aggregate 'converged' line), against the named observable below — EXCEPT `set_parent`'s
      epic case, which does NOT round-trip and is asserted directly against the transport with
      `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)`. That carve-out is not an exemption: routing it
      through the reconciler would make it untestable by construction, because
      `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` (dispatch_one.py:564) and only
      logs, so a swallowed failure is indistinguishable from success on the subprocess streams.

      **SCOPE EVERY MUTATION PASS WITH `--filter-local-ids`, OR IT WILL TRY TO CREATE THE WHOLE

      real project's, order 10^3 of them — down the CREATE path and attempts to file each one as a

      destroy the very isolation this story is built to prove. `--filter-local-ids <local_id>`
      (`__main__.py:520`, parsed at `:680-689`) scopes the pass to the cell's own ticket, so each
      cell touches exactly the one ticket it is asserting about. Two consequences to carry:
        * UNFILTERED passes are permitted in exactly TWO places, both DRY-RUN and therefore
          incapable of writing: the scrub-verification pass, and the pagination-recovery pass
          (which MUST be unfiltered — a filtered pass never crosses a page boundary and so
          cannot test paging at all). No unfiltered WRITING pass is ever run.
          (The store-copy check is a filesystem ticket
          count, not a pass at all, so it needs no scoping.)

          unfiltered one.

      UPDATE NEEDS A BINDING THE SCRUB HAS JUST REMOVED.** `outbound_differ.py:518-520` branches on

      no binding is never updated. Since the scrub deliberately strips every binding from the copied
      store, an outbound edit cell that just mutates a local ticket would CREATE a new DC issue —
      and then its oracle (`fields.summary` on 'the' DC issue) would happily pass against that
      freshly-created issue instead of the one the cell meant to change. Green, and proving nothing:
      the exact failure shape this story exists to end.
      So rows 2-13 (and outbound row 14) share ONE fixture, `bound_dc_issue(...)`, which:
        (1) creates a DC issue via `dc_transport.create_issue`;

            reason is easy to miss: there is NO inbound-only mode. Every writing mode

            so an unscoped pass over the scrubbed store would route its ~10^3 unbound tickets
            down the CREATE path — `bootstrap-strict` (cap=10, `mode.py:106`) would file 10

      dependent cell would fall back to the create path and pass for the wrong reason.
      Rows 1 (create) and inbound row 14 are the only cells that are structurally fine without it.

      issue in DC; (4) run the `--mode dry-run` pass and assert the probe entry. Skipping step 2

      nothing to do with the absence path — a false red that would read as a product defect.

      suite seeds at least `2 * observed + 1` issues IN THE HARNESS so at least three pages are
      required — pagination is a remote-side property and the store copy does not exercise it.

      seeding path is one the adapter actually supports), collecting the returned keys into a
      `seeded_keys` set. **This cell uses an UNFILTERED `--mode dry-run` pass — it is the one
      place a whole-store pass is required, and dry-run is what makes that safe.** Pagination is
      a property of the FETCH crossing page boundaries, so a filtered pass would scope to one id,
      never cross a boundary, and defeat the cell entirely; but an unfiltered WRITING pass would
      run the outbound differ over the scrubbed store and file spurious issues (see the scoping
      note above). Dry-run fetches every page and computes the plan while writing nothing, which
      is exactly what this criterion needs.
      `recovered_count` is therefore read from the PLAN, not from created tickets: the number of
      `seeded_keys` that appear as an inbound create entry in the envelope —
      `jq '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "inbound" and .action == "create")] | .[].local_id'`

      `recovered_count == len(seeded_keys)`. Counting recovered keys rather than total local

      assertion would be satisfied by the copy alone and would pass under exactly the truncation
      this criterion exists to catch.

      [rebar:21fc-51d7-90ca-4a03] existed.** The inbound pass finds issues through `fetcher._iter_pages`

      freshly seeded issues may not be searchable yet. A pass run immediately after seeding can
      therefore recover fewer than it should and fail with a TRUNCATION signature that is really
      index lag — the exact confusion that would send the next reader after a pagination bug that
      is not there. So the fixture must POLL the search until it returns all `seeded_keys` (with a
      bounded timeout that FAILS LOUDLY naming index lag) BEFORE the pass runs, and the cell must
      assert that precondition was met rather than assuming it.
